role_summary: Senior engineering leader who has personally built production GenAI systems in complex enterprise environments and led engineering organizations at scale. Must be hands-on enough to drive architectural decisions (RAG, agentic workflows, LLM deployment, evaluation frameworks) and senior enough to hold the room with a Fortune 500 CIO. The role leads Turing's forward-deployed engineering operation. The three core requirements are: (1) hands-on GenAI builder depth, (2) engineering leadership at organizational scale, and (3) experience building AI under the constraints of regulated or complex enterprise environments. Regulated verticals: BFSI is a priority but life sciences, retail/CPG, and other regulated industries are equally valid. Not a research role, not a pure management role, not a strategy role. This role has been in flux — originally scoped as 'Head of Applied AI Lab' with pure BFSI focus, now repositioned as Head of Forward Deployed Engineering with multi-vertical scope. Evaluate candidates against this brief, not the posted JD.
instructions: This brief deliberately avoids company-name anchoring. Do NOT use company names as search filters — use capability and delivery-context signals.

Vertical filtering happens at evaluation time, not search time. Search strings should target GenAI delivery capability, engineering leadership, and applied AI deployment language — not vertical-specific vocabulary.

Prioritize candidates from tech companies that SERVE regulated verticals over candidates FROM regulated vertical institutions. This is a preference, not a gate — someone at Goldman who was clearly a hands-on builder still qualifies.

The seniority sweet spot is Executive Director at a major bank equivalent. In tech: Director to Senior Director. VP at a growth-stage company is fine. VP at a large company is context-dependent. SVP/MD/Partner/C-suite at large org = too senior.

The title 'Forward Deployed Engineer' is Palantir-specific vocabulary. Most target candidates will NOT have this phrase in their profile. Search on the underlying capabilities: applied AI deployment, AI engineering leadership, GenAI platform engineering, applied AI architecture. Include client-facing delivery terms (solutions engineering, consulting engineering, delivery engineering) as additional search axes to expand the candidate pool.
Expect high noise on broad Recall strings — the three capability areas and depth distinction are the precision levers, not the search strings.
search_priorities: Directors / Senior Directors of AI / Engineering at enterprise AI companies who deploy into regulated clients
Directors / Heads of AI Engineering at Fortune 500 or large enterprises who built production GenAI systems — internal builders with engineering leadership and regulated vertical exposure
Heads of Engineering at applied AI startups building GenAI for BFSI, life sciences, or retail/CPG
Engineering Directors at consulting firms' AI engineering practices (build/deploy, not advisory)
VPs or Heads of AI at fintech / health-tech / retail-tech companies selling into or operating within regulated enterprises
Principal Engineers / Architects with both GenAI depth and engineering leadership at organizational scale
Engineering Directors / VPs at enterprise software or large tech companies who built production GenAI systems at scale
Forward Deployed Engineering leaders at companies like Palantir, Anduril, or similar models
intake_notes: Role has been a moving target for weeks. Originally 'Head of Applied AI Lab' with pure BFSI focus. Now 'Head of Forward Deployed Engineering' with multi-vertical scope (BFSI priority, life sciences, retail/CPG also accepted). Leveling: Executive Director at a major bank equivalent — no higher. A bit lower is okay. The search kit (ID: 10c0183e-f28b-49a0-b10f-680c73ab6fba) was built for the old BFSI-anchored framing and may need regeneration for the FDE framing. Use it if available but don't expect it to fully cover life sciences and retail/CPG vocabulary.

capability_areas.name: 1. Enterprise GenAI Delivery (HARD GATE)
capability_areas.description: Has personally architected and deployed GenAI systems in production enterprise environments. Not demos, not POCs that died, not strategy decks — systems that went live and stayed live. RAG pipelines, agentic workflows, copilots, orchestration frameworks, evaluation systems. This is the hard technical gate. Enterprise environment means Fortune 500, major financial institution, regulated industry, or enterprise-scale tech company — not a personal project or hackathon.
builder_signals: Specific GenAI tools personally used: LangGraph, LlamaIndex, DSPy, Haystack, CrewAI, Temporal, etc.
Action verbs with specificity: 'I architected a multi-agent system for...', 'I built the RAG pipeline that serves...', 'I deployed an evaluation framework across...'
Production deployment evidence: scale, latency requirements, uptime, user counts, throughput
Fine-tuned models, built RAG pipelines, designed agentic architectures, created evaluation frameworks THEMSELVES
GitHub contributions, technical blog posts, conference talks with architecture detail
Evidence of model selection, benchmarking, or evaluation design — not just using someone else's model
SENIOR LEADER SIGNALS (L8-L9): Led the AI function at a Fortune 500 or major financial institution
SENIOR LEADER SIGNALS (L8-L9): Directed $5M+ annual AI/R&D budgets
SENIOR LEADER SIGNALS (L8-L9): Built AI/R&D teams from scratch (domestic and/or global)
SENIOR LEADER SIGNALS (L8-L9): Translated R&D into products delivering measurable economic impact ($XM+)
SENIOR LEADER SIGNALS (L8-L9): Career arc from hands-on technical work (PhD, quant, engineering IC) into executive AI leadership
SENIOR LEADER SIGNALS (L8-L9): Pioneering or architecting next-generation AI paradigms (agentic AI, self-evolving systems, advanced optimization)
user_signals: Led team that built (managed builders, did not build personally)
Developed AI strategy (strategy without implementation evidence)
Adopted GitHub Copilot / Devin / off-the-shelf AI tools (tool adoption ≠ system building)
AI transformation officer / AI strategy lead framing without build evidence
Implemented vendor AI products (deployed Salesforce Einstein, not built custom AI)

capability_areas.name: 2. Vertical Domain Fluency
capability_areas.description: Has built AI systems that operated within the constraints of regulated or complex enterprise environments. The signal is NOT 'worked at Goldman' — it's 'built systems that had to satisfy compliance, audit, data governance, and regulatory requirements in a vertical context.' BFSI is a priority vertical but is NOT required — life sciences, retail/CPG, and other regulated industries are equally valid. The best signal is a tech company person who deployed INTO regulated verticals, but someone who built AI systems AT a regulated enterprise is also a strong signal. The key is: did they build under regulatory constraints?
builder_signals: Built AI for financial services — whether from the tech side deploying into banks/hedge funds/insurance OR as an engineer inside a financial institution building for internal platforms
Built AI under regulatory constraints: SOX, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FDA, GDPR applied to sensitive data
Deployed AI in environments with audit trail / explainability requirements
Experience with data governance in regulated contexts (data residency, PII handling, model governance, model risk management)
Worked at a tech company that sells into regulated verticals (Palantir, Dataiku, C3.ai, enterprise AI consultancies)
Built AI for life sciences: clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, drug discovery, medical NLP, FDA-compliant systems
Built AI for retail/CPG: demand forecasting, pricing optimization, supply chain AI at enterprise scale
Built AI at a Fortune 500 in any regulated industry — the regulatory constraint exposure is the signal, not the specific vertical
user_signals: Worked at a bank/pharma/retailer but in a non-technical capacity
Managed a data team at a vertical institution without personal technical depth
Vertical experience is entirely in unregulated tech (ad-tech, social media, gaming, consumer SaaS)

capability_areas.name: 3. Engineering Organization & Delivery Infrastructure Building
capability_areas.description: Has built the systems, processes, and organizational scaffolding that make engineering delivery repeatable at scale. Not just doing it once, but creating the infrastructure so a team can do it repeatedly. Reusable architectures, delivery playbooks, engineering standards, team scaling frameworks. This separates a senior IC who delivers well from a leader who builds a delivery organization. Lower priority than areas 1-2 but a strong differentiator between good and great candidates.
builder_signals: Built reusable GenAI reference architectures used across multiple projects or teams
Created delivery playbooks, engineering methodologies, or technical standards adopted by teams
Scaled an engineering or delivery org from small to large (e.g., 5 → 30 engineers)
Established engineering standards and quality processes for AI delivery
Built internal platforms, accelerators, or tooling that reduced time-to-deploy for GenAI solutions
Created repeatable processes for technical engagements, onboarding, or cross-team collaboration
Stood up an AI practice, center of excellence, or engineering function from scratch
user_signals: Only ever delivered bespoke one-off solutions with no repeatability
Managed delivery operations but didn't build the operational infrastructure or technical standards
Strategy consulting on 'how to build a practice' without actually building one

post_save_modifiers.name: Client-Facing / Forward-Deployed Delivery Experience
post_save_modifiers.trigger: Candidate has been evaluated as SAVE, SIGNAL_SAVE, TRANSFERABLE_SAVE, or INFERENTIAL_SAVE based on the three core capability areas
post_save_modifiers.if_present: Boost confidence by 0.05-0.10. Note in evidence: 'Client-facing delivery experience present — confidence boosted.' This is a differentiator that increases the candidate's value, not a criterion that contributed to the save decision.
post_save_modifiers.if_absent: No adjustment. The save decision stands on the three core capability areas. Do not note the absence of client-facing experience as a gap, limitation, or concern.
signals: Led engineering teams embedded at client sites or working directly on client infrastructure
Personally scoped and delivered technical solutions for external enterprise clients
Built repeatable delivery playbooks from client engagements
Experience at enterprise AI companies with professional services / forward-deployed models (Palantir, Dataiku, C3.ai, ThoughtSpot, etc.)
Experience at consulting firms with real engineering delivery (not just advisory)
Managed delivery against client timelines, budgets, and requirements

depth_distinction.builder_definition: Has personally architected and deployed GenAI systems in production enterprise environments. 'Personally' means: made the architectural decisions, wrote or reviewed critical code, designed the evaluation framework, drove technical conversations with engineering stakeholders. The whiteboard test: could this person diagram a production RAG + agentic architecture, explain the tradeoffs they made, and defend their design choices against a skeptical CTO? 'Deployed' means: the system went to production in an enterprise environment, not a demo, not a POC that died, not an internal prototype. Evidence: specific tool names, production metrics, deployment context, business outcomes. FOR L8-L9 CANDIDATES: 'Builder' also means: built and led the AI function at an enterprise, directed multi-million-dollar AI R&D budgets, built AI teams from scratch, set technical direction at the architecture level, and drove R&D-to-production translation with measurable economic impact. At this seniority, the whiteboard test is met by career trajectory (PhD + quant/engineering IC + executive AI leadership) combined with scope evidence (budget authority, team building, production impact). Tool names and explicit 'I built' language are bonuses at L8-L9, not requirements.
depth_distinction.user_definition: Manages, directs, or strategizes about AI systems without personal technical involvement in their design or implementation. This includes: leading the team that built it without personal technical depth, developing AI strategy or transformation roadmaps, adopting vendor AI tools (GitHub Copilot, Devin, Salesforce Einstein), managing AI product portfolios, overseeing AI initiatives from a CXO/VP seat. The distinguishing question: if the engineering team disappeared tomorrow, could this person personally build a working production GenAI system? If not, they're a user.

evidence_tiers.tier_1_direct: Explicit builder evidence — specific GenAI tool names (LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, etc.), production metrics, 'I built/architected/deployed' language, GitHub contributions, technical blog posts with architecture detail. This is the strongest evidence and sufficient at any seniority level.
evidence_tiers.tier_2_positional: Scope and role evidence — led the AI function at a Fortune 500 or major institution, directed $5M+ AI/R&D budgets, built AI/R&D teams from scratch, translated R&D into products with measurable economic impact ($XM+). At L8-L9 seniority, Tier 2 evidence is sufficient for a SAVE when combined with a technical career foundation (engineering IC, PhD, quant background).
evidence_tiers.tier_3_trajectory: Career arc evidence — PhD from a top-tier institution + engineering/quant IC career + progressive executive AI leadership across multiple major employers. At L8-L9, Tier 3 alone can justify a SAVE when the trajectory is unambiguous (e.g., PhD Cornell → quant → VP JPMorgan → Head of AI at Fortune 500 → Senior Research Scientist at Amazon). The logic: someone who rose through technical ranks to lead AI at major institutions did not do so without building.

depth_distinction.edge_case_guidance: STARTUP CTOs: CTO at a small company (<150 employees) who personally architects the system AND leads the team is a BUILDER — apply the Jon Dorando principle. CTO at a large company (400+ engineering org) is almost certainly a USER at this point — too far from the code. VP / HEAD OF at a mid-size company: context-dependent, look for evidence of recent hands-on work (PRs, architecture docs, technical blog posts). CONSULTING DIRECTORS: Directors at consulting firms can be either — some are delivery engineers who also manage, some are practice leaders who sell and staff. Look for builder signals in their project descriptions, not their title. CAREER ARC AND RECENCY: At L8-L9 seniority, most candidates will have transitioned from hands-on coding to architectural leadership and team direction. This is expected and acceptable. 'Builder' at L8-L9 does NOT require recent pull requests — it requires evidence that the person can still drive architectural decisions and engage at the technical level. A career arc from PhD/engineering IC → technical leadership → executive AI leadership IS builder evidence (Tier 3). The Hungjen Wang calibration example illustrates this: PhD → quant roles → VP JPMorgan → Head of AI at Franklin Templeton → Senior Research Scientist at Amazon — trajectory alone justifies SAVE. SAAS PRODUCT COMPANIES SERVING REGULATED ENTERPRISES: A Head of Engineering at a health-tech SaaS company that sells FDA-compliant AI products to hospitals is a strong fit. The signal is: built production AI under regulatory constraints for enterprise customers. Whether delivery was on-site or via SaaS product is a business model distinction, not a capability distinction.

inferential_save_rules.description: For profiles where evidence is sparse but priors are strong, the agent should SAVE with a flag rather than REJECT on insufficient evidence. These candidates get passed to the recruiter for manual review.
conditions: Director/Head of AI or Engineering at a known enterprise AI company (Palantir, Dataiku, C3.ai, etc.) with GenAI keywords in headline — even without detailed summary bullets
Engineering leader at a company known for deploying AI into enterprise environments with 12+ years experience — even if profile is sparse on specifics
Profile shows clear progression from hands-on engineering into engineering leadership with GenAI in the most recent role — even if profile is sparse on details
CTO/VP Engineering at a small AI startup (<150 employees) serving regulated verticals — even if profile lacks detail

Head of AI / VP of AI / Chief AI Architect at a Fortune 500 or major financial institution with 15+ years experience and evidence of team-building and R&D-to-production translation — even without explicit GenAI tool names

PhD from a top-tier institution (MIT, Stanford, CMU, Berkeley, etc.) + executive AI leadership at multiple major employers + currently at a top-tier research organization (Amazon, Google, Meta, etc.) — trajectory alone justifies SAVE for L8-L9 roles (Tier 3 evidence)
Engineering leader (Director+) at a Fortune 500 or major enterprise company with GenAI keywords in headline and 12+ years experience — even if profile is sparse on specifics
inferential_save_rules.note: The intersection of GenAI builder + regulated vertical experience + NYC + 12yr+ is extremely narrow. Err on the side of saving ambiguous profiles that hit 2 of 3 core requirements (CA1 GenAI depth, engineering leadership, regulated vertical). The recruiter would rather review 5 borderline candidates than miss 1 real one in a market this sparse.

non_fit_patterns.label: Solutions Architect at cloud vendor
non_fit_patterns.description: Solutions Architects at AWS, Azure, or GCP who do customer-facing pre-sales demos and architecture reviews. They show products to clients, they don't build production systems.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Customer-facing pre-sales and demos, not production AI engineering delivery. The role requires someone who BUILDS the system, not someone who demos the vendor's capabilities.
examples: Head of Customer Solutions / Sr. Leader Solutions Architecture @ AWS

non_fit_patterns.label: Head of AI Products / VP AI Products / Product Manager of AI
non_fit_patterns.description: Product management layer over engineering. They define what to build, not how to build it. Even at regulated vertical firms, this is a fundamentally different skill set.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Product managers direct engineering, they don't do engineering. The role needs someone who can personally drive architectural decisions, not someone who writes product requirements.
examples: Executive Director & Head of AI Products @ JPMorgan
SVP Data & Analytics Product Manager @ Citi

non_fit_patterns.label: AI Transformation Executive / AI Strategy Lead
non_fit_patterns.description: Strategy and transformation framing without implementation evidence. The higher the title at a large org, the further from building.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Strategy without implementation is the opposite of what this role needs. The role delivers working systems, not transformation roadmaps.

non_fit_patterns.label: C-suite / SVP / MD at large org
non_fit_patterns.description: CTO of a 400+ person engineering org, CDAO, CIO, EVP, SVP, MD at a major bank, Partner at Big4. Too senior for the scope and comp ceiling. The bigger the org they ran, the further from hands-on work.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Scope and comp ceiling mismatch. The role needs someone who still gets their hands dirty with architecture and code. Someone running a 400-person engineering org hasn't reviewed a PR in years.
examples: CTO Investments & Capital Markets @ Freddie Mac (400-person org)

non_fit_patterns.label: AI experience = tool adoption, not system building
non_fit_patterns.description: AI involvement limited to rolling out vendor tools: GitHub Copilot adoption, Devin integration, Salesforce Einstein implementation, or similar off-the-shelf AI deployment. This is IT enablement, not AI engineering.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Implementing vendor AI tools requires evaluation and rollout skills, not architecture and engineering skills. The role builds custom GenAI systems from scratch.
examples: CTO who 'implemented GitHub Copilot and Devin across engineering'
VP who 'led AI transformation through vendor tool adoption'

non_fit_patterns.label: Customer Success / Pre-Sales adjacent
non_fit_patterns.description: Client-facing roles focused on adoption, demos, and account management rather than engineering delivery. They help clients USE products, not build custom systems.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: Client-facing but not engineering. The role requires someone who architects and deploys, not someone who coaches and demos.
examples: Customer Success Director for AI products

non_fit_patterns.label: Career entirely in unregulated tech verticals
non_fit_patterns.description: All experience is in ad-tech, social media, gaming, consumer SaaS, or other verticals with no regulatory, compliance, or data governance complexity.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: No exposure to the constraints that define delivery in regulated enterprises. Building AI without regulatory constraints is a fundamentally different discipline. Not auto-skip if GenAI depth and engineering leadership are exceptional, but a significant gap.
examples: Director of ML at a social media company
Head of AI at a gaming studio
VP Engineering at an ad-tech company

non_fit_patterns.label: Solo boutique consultant / fractional executive
non_fit_patterns.description: Founder of a 1-person consulting shop or fractional CTO practice. May have deep knowledge but no evidence of building or leading a delivery organization at scale.
non_fit_patterns.why_not: The role leads a team and builds a practice. Solo consulting demonstrates individual expertise but not the team leadership and practice-building the role requires.

non_fit_override_rule: A non-fit pattern is OVERRIDDEN if the candidate's profile shows specific evidence of work in a capability area at the builder level. The non-fit label describes default expectations for a title/company combination; actual evidence in summary bullets always wins. When evidence contradicts the non-fit pattern, note the conflict and evaluate on evidence. 'Career in unregulated verticals' is overridden if the candidate's GenAI depth and engineering leadership are exceptional enough to compensate for the vertical gap.

employer_signal_rules.evidence_required: Engineering leadership role (Director+) at an enterprise AI company that deploys into client environments. These companies' operating model IS forward-deployed engineering. Title + company is a strong signal. Verify GenAI depth (some of these companies predate the GenAI era — look for post-2022 GenAI work).

Engineering delivery role at a consulting firm — NOT advisory/strategy, NOT partner level. Titles like Technology Fellow, Director of AI Engineering, Lead Solutions Architect WITH build evidence. The key distinction: did they BUILD and DEPLOY, or did they ADVISE and STAFF? Many consulting profiles will look like fits but are actually strategy/advisory. CA1 (technical depth) is the critical filter. Partner-level at Big4 = too senior regardless.

AI startups (<200 employees) serving BFSI, life sciences, or retail/CPG clients. Not name-limited. Engineering leadership at these companies combines tech-side operating culture with vertical domain exposure. Verify GenAI depth (post-2022). CTO or Head of Engineering at these companies is a strong signal IF they're hands-on (apply the <150 employee CTO rule).

Candidates FROM regulated vertical institutions (banks, pharma, insurers, retailers, Fortune 500) who were clearly BUILDERS — hands-on engineering leaders who built production AI/GenAI systems. This tier is intentionally not name-limited. The test: did they build the AI system or manage the people who built it? Titles like Engineering Director, Head of AI Engineering, Sr Principal Engineer, Principal Architect at a bank/pharma/retailer/Fortune 500 WITH builder evidence pass. Titles like CTO, CDAO, SVP, MD at these institutions are almost certainly too senior. VP is context-dependent.

Tech companies focused on regulated verticals — fintechs, health-tech companies, retail-tech platforms. Not name-limited. Engineering leadership at these companies combines tech-side operating culture with vertical domain exposure. Verify GenAI depth (post-2022).

Same standard as any candidate — all three capability areas evaluated on evidence. Candidates from companies not in the above tiers can absolutely be strong fits — the tiers are signal strength boosters, not gates.

minimum_bar_description: 12+ years total experience with GenAI builder depth, engineering leadership at organizational scale, and NYC location. The hard bar is: (1) hands-on GenAI architecture experience (CA1), (2) engineering leadership at organizational scale, and (3) regulated vertical exposure (CA2). A 12-year IC with no leadership does not qualify — the role requires both technical depth and organizational leadership. The years floor exists to ensure the candidate has the seniority to hold credibility with Fortune 500 CIOs, not as an arbitrary gate. Post-2022 GenAI work is required — pre-LLM ML experience is valuable context but insufficient alone. NYC metro location is non-negotiable.

author: Sam Vangelos
notes: V4 brief for Head of Forward Deployed Engineering. Structural rewrite of v3 to eliminate the 'defensive negation architecture' problem — where every 'DO NOT reject for lacking client-facing experience' kept 'client-facing as criterion' salient in the model's attention. Key changes from v3: (1) REMOVED Capability Area 2 (Client-Facing / Forward-Deployed Engineering Leadership) entirely — client-facing delivery is no longer evaluated as a capability area, (2) ADDED post_save_modifiers — client-facing delivery is now a post-save confidence modifier that only fires AFTER a save decision has been made on the three core CAs, making it architecturally impossible for client-facing absence to trigger a rejection, (3) RENUMBERED remaining CAs: Vertical Domain Fluency is now CA2, Engineering Org Building is now CA3, (4) REMOVED instruction #7 (the 'CRITICAL EVALUATION RULE' about not rejecting for lacking client-facing) — unnecessary when client-facing isn't evaluated as a capability area, (5) REMOVED all defensive negation language ('do NOT reject for lacking...', 'NOT a gate', 'its ABSENCE is never a reason to reject') — replaced with positive framing of what IS required, (6) ADDED additional_search_terms — client-facing vocabulary preserved for search expansion but separated from evaluation criteria, (7) MERGED fast_exit_patterns and trajectory_no_patterns into fast_exit — these were redundant, (8) ADDED trajectory_no_pattern for client-facing titles WITHOUT GenAI keywords — client-facing context alone is insufficient without technical depth, (9) CLEANED calibration examples — internal builder archetype now explains the post_save_modifier pattern instead of using defensive language, (10) CLEANED employer_signal_rules — removed 'regardless of delivery model' hedging, (11) CLEANED inferential_save_rules — removed delivery model references. Design principle: positive framing over negative instructions, architectural impossibility over prompt discipline. The core requirements are three things: hands-on GenAI builder depth, engineering leadership at organizational scale, regulated vertical exposure. Everything else is a modifier.
